tagline.text: The National Artist's own works and Cordillera art in one museum

location.label: Location
location.text: Km. 6 Asin Road, Tadiangan, Tuba, Benguet

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱200–700 (including admission; check café prices on site, per person)

children.text: The BenCab Museum was founded by the Philippine National Artist Benedicto "BenCab" Cabrera and sits on a hill in Tuba, about a 15-minute drive from central Baguio. It shows his own works, Cordillera indigenous art and contemporary art, and also has a farm and garden with an eco-trail past Ifugao and Kalinga houses.

The BenCab Museum stands beside Asin Road in Tuba, Benguet, on a hill slightly west of central Baguio. It was founded by the National Artist Benedicto "BenCab" Cabrera, who also serves as its curator; construction began in 2006 and it opened in 2009. The BenCab Art Foundation owns and runs it. It is about a
15–20 minute
drive from central Baguio.

BenCab was born on April 10, 1942, in Malabon, Rizal. He earned a bachelor's degree in fine arts at the University of the Philippines Diliman in 1963 and was named National Artist for Visual Arts (Painting) in 2006. After returning from Europe he settled in Baguio, where he keeps a studio and farm in Tuba, co-founded the Baguio Arts Guild (serving as its president in 1991), and helped create Tam-awan Village. His Larawan series grew out of his collection of early maps and prints of the Philippines.

The building has four levels and is divided into several galleries: the BenCab Gallery, Cordillera Gallery, Erotica Gallery, Philippine Contemporary Art Gallery, Sepia Gallery, Maestro Gallery, Print Gallery, Patio Salvador and Larawan Hall. Together they hold BenCab's own works, Cordillera indigenous art that he considers underappreciated, and works by other artists who caught his eye. The museum also holds paintings, sculptures and installations alongside indigenous artifacts from the Cordillera, and has a space for temporary exhibitions. Admission covers the galleries, while the eco-trail has a separate fee plus a guide fee. On the eco-trail, a guide accompanies groups of 10 for children aged 6 to 12 and groups of 15 for visitors aged 13 and up.

Beyond the galleries lies the BenCab Farm & Garden. There is an eco-trail past Igorot houses that reflect Ifugao, Kalinga and Bontoc architecture, and the grounds include a farm growing coffee and other crops and a bonsai garden. You can eat and drink at Café Sabel, the restaurant and café on the grounds.

This gallery gathers the works of the National Artist BenCab. One visitor account mentions a portrait of Sabel, his muse, and a self-portrait on the walls, and the paintings on display are said to be a private collection that is not for sale.

This gallery presents the Cordillera indigenous art and artifacts that BenCab considers underappreciated. Artifacts such as a hagabi bench, carved from a single piece of wood and said to have been used by Ifugao nobility, have been shown here. Displays can change.
This gallery gathers works on the theme of erotica. Some pieces may be adult in nature, so check ahead if you are visiting with children.

blocks.title: Philippine contemporary art and Maestro galleries

children.text: These galleries show works by other Philippine artists. The Philippine Contemporary Art Gallery and the Maestro Gallery are separate, and the Maestro Gallery has hosted works by masters such as Araceli Limcaco Dans, Arturo Luz and Jose Joya.

These galleries gather prints and sepia-toned works. According to a visitor account, 18th- and 19th-century Philippine prints have been shown here, including eruptions of Mayon, Taal and Camiguin volcanoes, old Manila and provincial scenes. Displays vary over time.
These are the Patio Salvador and Larawan Hall inside the building. They are spaces where you can rest between galleries.
This forest path follows Igorot houses that reflect Ifugao, Kalinga and Bontoc architecture. Guided tours are available, and you also see a coffee farm, a bonsai garden and a pond with ducks and koi.

This is the restaurant and café on the grounds, overlooking the farm and garden. Outside food cannot be brought in, and food and drink are allowed only here. Visitors say you can buy fish feed for the koi pond at the café.
Enter when the museum opens. Leave large bags at the entrance and take photos without flash.
Go through the galleries in order starting from the lowest level, and see the BenCab Gallery and the Cordillera Gallery.
Tour the Philippine Contemporary Art, Maestro, Sepia and Print galleries.
Have lunch and a rest at Café Sabel.
Head out to the farm and garden and walk the eco-trail. You can also sign up for a guided tour.
Take one more turn around the garden and browse the museum shop for souvenirs.
The last entry is at
. If you are short on time, choose either the galleries or the eco-trail and focus on that.

items.title: One day in Baguio
items.subtitle: Building the day around the museum

children.text: Have breakfast in downtown Baguio and take a light walk around
Burnham Park
Go to the BenCab Museum by jeepney or taxi. It takes about
15–20 minutes
by car from downtown.
Tour the galleries and walk the eco-trail. The rules are strict, so turn off your flash and leave your bag at the reception counter.
Have lunch at Café Sabel and browse the museum shop.
Return to town, walk around
Session Road
and have dinner.
The museum is closed on Mondays, so switch to a town-based plan on Mondays.
From Manila, take a long-distance bus such as Victory Liner to Baguio. The trip usually takes
4.5–5.5 hours
and a one-way ticket costs about
If you drive, take NLEX and TPLEX up to Baguio.
Bus times and fares change, so check the operator's latest announcements.
It is about a
15-minute
drive from downtown Baguio, and traffic can stretch it to about
20 minutes
By public transport, take a jeepney marked "Asin" from the jeepney terminal near Baguio Market.
Taxis can be found anywhere in town, and fares vary with traffic, so confirm the fare before you get in.
Taxis and Grab are also available. You can also catch a jeepney that passes the museum from the terminal on Otek Street or on Kayang Street across from City Hall.
Coming back, you need to flag down a passing jeepney or taxi, so it is safer to leave before dark. Check the latest announcements for opening hours and closing days.
The address is Km. 6 Asin Road, Tadiangan, Tuba (near the Kilometer 91 marker).
The museum's own directions also say it is about
15 minutes
by car from downtown Baguio.

The museum is mostly indoors, so you can enjoy it on rainy days too. For the eco-trail and the garden, though, the dry season from November to May is more comfortable. Baguio is high enough to stay cool even at midday, and in February the Panagbenga Flower Festival crowds the city, so the quiet of the museum can be a welcome change.
The museum opens at
and is closed on Mondays. Weekends and holidays are crowded, so go on a weekday morning if you want to see it at a relaxed pace.

The cool highland air makes walking pleasant even at midday, but the outdoor eco-trail can be slippery after rain. On rainy days, concentrate on the galleries, and on clear days spend more time on the eco-trail and in the garden.

items.label: General admission
items.note: Free for children 42 inches (about 107 cm) or shorter

items.label: Meal at Café Sabel
items.note: The only food and drink area in the museum

children.text: Prices are approximate as of

Food and drink inside the museum are available only at Café Sabel. Outside food and drink cannot be brought in, so plan to have lunch here. Check on site whether the café is open, and its menu and prices. Café Sabel overlooks the farm and garden on the grounds, and visitors say you can rest while watching the ducks and koi in the pond.
Lodging is concentrated in downtown Baguio, so most visitors see the museum on a half-day trip from town.
When choosing lodging, base yourself in downtown Baguio. The area around
Burnham Park
and
Session Road
has restaurants and conveniences nearby, and it is easy to catch a jeepney or taxi to the museum from there. If you want a light bite before or after your visit, you can do it in this area.
The museum is open Tuesday to Sunday from
to
, with last entry at
. It is closed on Mondays, Christmas Day and New Year's Day.
Large bags and bulky items must be left at the reception counter at the entrance.
Personal still photography is allowed, but flash, video recording, drones, tripods and monopods are prohibited. Selfie sticks are allowed only in the farm and garden.
Do not touch artworks or artifacts, or lean on pedestals or walls. Keep about 30 cm (12 inches) away from the artworks.
Sketching is allowed in pencil only, in sketchbooks no larger than 8.5 × 11 inches.
Eco-trail guides accompany groups of 10 children aged 6 to 12 and groups of 15 visitors aged 13 and up. This costs extra on top of admission, so decide in advance whether to include it.
Check the museum's official website or Facebook page for the latest fees and hours.
The museum shop reportedly sells art and culture books and locally made handicrafts, including toys.
Visitors report that parking for private cars is limited, so on weekends public transport or a taxi may be easier.
You are told you can catch a jeepney that passes the museum from the Otek Street terminal in downtown Baguio (near Good Taste Restaurant) or from Kayang Street across from Baguio City Hall.
Outside food and drink and pets are not allowed, and smoking is prohibited throughout the grounds. Management may remove disruptive visitors.
Children must be supervised by an adult at all times, and shouting and running are prohibited.
To protect the artworks, flash photography and video recording are prohibited.
Management may restrict access to some areas as needed, and visitors are responsible for their own safety.
CCTV cameras are in operation.
The eco-trail can be slippery on rainy days, so wear shoes with good grip.
The museum is closed on Mondays, Christmas Day and New Year's Day, so check this when you plan your schedule.
This highland city is about a
15-minute
drive from the museum. Continue your sightseeing and meals in Baguio.
A farm that is a good stop in strawberry season.
A park in the center of Baguio, good for a walk around the lake after the museum.
Baguio's main street, lined with restaurants and shops.
An art village built in the style of a traditional Cordillera village, which BenCab helped create. It is in Pinsao, northwest of downtown Baguio.
